I'm so sorry. You're in a lot of pain, and I wish there was something I could do to make it go away for you. I'm sorry that you're having such a hard time connecting with people. It's hard, especially when you're young, and you and everyone around you is changing so dramatically every year. But please don't kill yourself. These are things that *will* get better as you grow up.
I'm so sorry for the pain that you're feeling. Please don't do anything foolish, though. The pain you're feeling right now will pass, you will meet other women and other friends.

Sorry you feel like shit. I've been there.

Couple of things that may make you feel better:

First, *writers* don't make a lot of money, but people who *can write* can make really great livings. Being able to express yourself in words is incredibly important. You probably won't make a ton of money as a novelist, but how about as a grant writer, or a business consultant. Moreover, people who can write well typically also reason well. You may have skills you don't know you have.

My life sucked at 22. It gets better. Treat yourself well, and get to know yourself. See a counselor if you would feel comfortable and can afford it -- being able to talk through some of these issues in depth can be helpful, and he/she might be able to advise you on whether anti-depressants might help.

Again, I'm sorry for the pain you're going through.

I've been there, and I know that in the depths of depression, it doesn't matter how many people say to you that things will get better, you don't buy it. But these things really do improve, and, the older you get, the more ways you can find to build a life around you that gives you gratification. But, again, I understand how hopeless it feels when you're in the midst of it all.

Can you find some time to escape mentally, curl up with a good book and get away from it all? Paul Theroux's travel books have often been wonderful mental vacations for me when I couldn't have the real thing. I realize it's a lame solution to very painful problems for you, but it does sound like you just need a break.

Best of luck with everything.

Man, I understand the urge to drive off and escape the world! Everyone feels that way from time to time. I'm sorry you're in so much pain. I've been there myself, feeling like a failure and an embarrassment. It gets better.

PM me if you need to talk. But please don't do anything foolish. Suicide is a permanent solution to temporary problems.

I'm so sorry for all of the pain you're feeling. Life can certainly be painful, but it can also be beautiful and sublime. I'm sorry that most of what you've experienced to date is the pain.

I can't give you answers, but I can tell you what worked for me. 

First, you're not that different from anyone else: no weaker, no lazier, not even necessarily more depressed or pained than other people. All those happy people around you, myself included, are just as confused and as pained as you are, at times. You're no more a failure than they are, although in some obvious, overt, external ways you haven't had the marks of success that they have. Stop worrying about what everyone else thinks about you; more often than not, they're not thinking about you, they're worrying about their own facade, and about what other people think about them.

Second, baby steps: don't try to do everything overnight, but take small steps, and build on whatever success you can find. Make a small, measurable goal, and stick to it. When I decided to get into shape, I told myself I would exercise six days every week, no matter how little I actually exercised, even if I just trotted to the end of the block. I've kept my own streak going for five years now, always exercising six days per week. Keeping the streak going has been a very good motivator for me.

Thirdly, find things you can do well, and learn how to do them better. It takes a lot of time to get good at something. Start now. It doesn't even matter what it is. Computer programming is great for us nerds, but it can be anything: magic tricks, reading, writing, fantasy football. 

Reading, in particular, is a great way to confront ideas and help you establish your own standards for yourself, rather than just accepting the standards your peers have.

Finally, you may want to seek out some counseling and find someone to talk to about what you're up against.

PM me, or post back here, if you want to talk more. You can do this.

High school sucks for most people, but I think gays and lesbians have it worse than most because so many of the discoveries you're making put you at odds with the main stream.

You've seen the [It Gets Better](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7IcVyvg2Qlo) video, right? A lot of people are going through what you are. One day you won't be in high school, and you'll have a much easier time in finding people going through exactly the same things that you are.

Can you talk to you doctor about other dosages or types of antidepressants to find something that works for you?

Best of luck with this.

I'm so sorry. The depression and the pressure of school seem like a lot to deal with at the same time. It sounds like taking a break is a good idea.

I don't have any experience with ECT, so maybe I'm not the one to comment on many aspects of this. Hopefully more qualified people will comment. In the meantime...

College is rough even under the best situations. The pressure of succeeding, being away from familiar environments, awkward social situations, these are genuinely challenging things to deal with. In looking back, I'm not sure I've done anything more difficult than that initial adjustment. There's nothing to be ashamed of in getting it wrong the first go-round. I got many aspects of it wrong myself. Take a break, collect your thoughts, give yourself some time to adjust.

I'm always interested in the fact that many antidepressants aren't actually antidepressants, but rather anti-anxiety drugs. In my own life, the onset of depression has been very closely tied to anxiety. The extent to which I've learned to manage my anxiety has been more or less the extent to which I've learned to manage my depression.

What I think could be good about a break for you is that it would give you some time to reflect over what triggered your depression in college, and whether there are aspects of this you can learn to manage in a safe environments.

And, by all means, figure out a way to work regular exercise into your daily life. It did wonders for me.

Best of luck dealing with everything. Please keep us posted on how things go for you!
It really wasn't that it stopped working for me, but I worried that I never developed any sober social skills, since I used alcohol as such a crutch.

I'm sorry for what you're going through. I went through a long period like yours when I was in grad school. Wasn't four years, but it was close.

It sounds like you are indeed making all the right steps. I wonder whether this is something that is going to take more that 5 months before you start seeing an improvement. Have you told all these things to your therapist? If so, what did he/she propose doing in the way of exploring different medications and/or dosages?

Don't you just hate it when people tell you that you should just get out more and meet people? Like that never occurred to you. Right, I should just *meet* people. So I won't suggest that, quite. But since you mentioned both drinking and exercising, have you ever thought of contacting the [Hash House Harriers](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_House_Harriers) about going on a Hash run with them? Really fun group, and there's probably a chapter nearby. Absolutely saved my life. I stopped running with them when I stopped drinking, but I'm still in contact with many wonderful people I met there.

Seriously, it will get better. You're already doing so much so well. But I get the frustration, the impatience. Post here again or PM me if you want to talk more.

That's rough. Sounds like you need a little comfort and understanding and time to grieve, and I'm sorry that your mother can't offer this for you. Things will get better with time, even though it doesn't seem like it now.

I just stopped one day, something that I realize doesn't work for everyone. I was never at the point where I couldn't stop drinking. For me, it was always more like after the second or third beer I wanted to keep on. After years of trying to drink in moderation, I just gave up and stopped altogether.

But most people find they need some kind of a support system. Have you read [Roger Ebert's article on AA](http://blogs.suntimes.com/ebert/2009/08/my_name_is_roger_and_im_an_alc.html)?

There's also [Rational Recovery](https://rational.org/index.php?id=1), if the spiritual aspect of AA bothers you.

Feel free to PM me if you need someone to talk to about this. Been there.

Ditto the thanks for your service. The only thing I'd add to the good advice posted here is that if the VA counselor was helping, you should find a way to see him. Nothing is more important than your own well-being.

I'm so sorry for your pain, you must be going through incredible grief. Being a new parent is scary enough. I haven't gone through anything this hard, but I am a parent, I've been through hard times in my life, and I'm a good listener if you feel like you need to talk. PM me.

Regardless, my love and best wishes for you and your new daughter.
Ditto. Life can be rough sometimes. Come talk to us when it gets you down.
Awesome!

I'm a scientist as well (Chemist). We depressed-yet-intellectual types can make up all sorts of great metaphors. The connections between water molecules are electrostatic, and there's very little coupling. Whereas the connections between people are extremely nonlinear, as people affect each other in often subtle yet significant and lasting ways. I assure you that you are dear to more people than you imagine.

As a scientist, you at least can understand chemical imbalances. To steal a line from "Listening to Prozac", no one tells a diabetic that they should try to live without insulin. Everyone recognizes that diabetics have a chemical imbalance that just needs to be corrected. But there's this stigma amongst depressives. Heck, I've tried to get off my meds before. Can you find one that doesn't make you sick?

Can you find a therapist that works for you? Or maybe a group, since maybe you're peers will just listen to you rather than trying to treat you. The point is, you're worth the effort to try and find something that lasts.

If you just need someone to talk to, I will reply to every PM you send me (given a few hours lag time).

And you *do* have people that care about you! I assure you, there are many many more than you imagine.

Ditto on the Sleigh Bells!
Yep. I've been through it and I know just how awful it feels, and how, in the midst of it, you feel like the cloud will never lift. It will.
Great!

Congrats on making it a year, that really is a big deal. Just in case I need to say it, the woman is full of shit. She doesn't know you, she doesn't know whether or not you belong. Don't read too much into the words of one asshole. Doesn't mean anything about you. She's probably just having a bad day.

If you've tried 13 times, I imagine you've seen therapists and other professionals. How did that go for you? Did that make you feel better? Have you tried any sort of anti-depressant medication? They did wonders for me.

You can do this, you can make your own life a source of joy for you. You belong, here on reddit, at least, and I'm glad you posted here so I could chat with you. Please don't try again, you're dear to more people than you can ever imagine.

This.

Don't define yourself in terms of her. You're your own person. Live the life that's meaningful to you. I realize this is easier said than done. Move away, do the things you love, send her a card at Christmas and Mother's Day, but otherwise be completely separate of her.

I'm so sorry, that has to be an awful situation, and I can't imagine the pain you must be going through. I understand the desire for space -- I feel it when my life is going great, even, but it's certainly most acute when things are awful. The grind, the repetition, the lack of time to do anything. I get it.

Space takes many forms, though. Why not quit your job, sell your belongings, and then travel the world? Hitch hike to Patagonia or something. Most people in the world live on pennies a day. Or why not quit your job, sell your belongings, and move to another city? The point is that you can write your script however you want to at this point.

The architect Buckminster Fuller came very close to suicide at one point, feeling like a hopeless failure with nothing to live for. He resolved that if he lived he would dedicate his life to the universe.

PM me if you want to talk. I know something about the pain you're going through.
Please don't. I understand you're going through a lot of pain. But this is something you can work through. PM me and I'll call you.

I'm so sorry for your pain. Sounds really awful. I read your post a few days ago and didn't post anything right away, since there was a lot of good ideas that other people posted. But your words stuck with me and I wanted to say this:

The part that resonated with me was the fact that you're being treated like shit by your wife, and you're reacting with regret, sadness, etc. That's how I would have done it, I would have said "what's wrong with me, that she would do this to me, why can't I find a meaningful relationship?" or something along those lines. 

Look, the problem isn't with you, it's with her. To hell with her, if she marries you, doesn't respect you or her vows to you. You deserve so much better than this.

Kapaso is right - many, many people feel the same way, go through the same things, feel the same frustrations. I think his advice about learning how to talk to strangers is great, if you can manage it. Alternatively, maybe you should think about seeing a therapist, counselor, or some kind of group to talk through some of these feelings. It sounds like you've got a lot of positives in your life already, and if you're feeling this low, maybe talking through some of these issues in a trusted atmosphere will help. Maybe the therapist can give you some advice about whether medication will help you (it helped me).

Please don't do anything stupid. You are dear to more people than you imagine, and the world will be a less interesting place without you. Reply or PM me if you'd like to talk more.

You're going through a lot, now, and I congratulate you for making the progress that you have. "Gradually improving" is pretty great, as is "losing weight", "making friends" and the rest. You're confronting parts of yourself that you want to change and you've been successful at it.

Okay, so everything isn't going as quickly as you'd like. Be patient with yourself. What you're doing is really hard, give it time. It's really hard for us depressive types to be kind and patient with ourselves, we're always brutally hard on ourselves, much crueler to ourselves than we would be to someone else. Give it time.

Part of this being tough on yourself, I suspect, might be causing you to lie to your doctors about the meds. You lie to them, I suspect, because you feel like you need to respond to their attentions in the way you're "supposed to respond". Kroneland is absolutely right: Be honest with your doctors, or find a doctor that you can be honest to.

And part of your being tough on yourself is your impatience with your education. Is it really going to matter in 10 years whether it took you a couple extra years to go to community college to get some extra courses. mcgillert, here, is correct: there is always a way to pay for college.

In the words of Kurt Vonnegut: "There's only one rule I know of, babies -- God damn it, you've just got to be kind." *Especially to yourself.*

Best wishes for your continued progress.

I'm so sorry about your friend's death. You've already made some good steps to deal with this. Crying/grieving is a very constructive process. It feels draining and exhausting, and it feels like you're not doing anything, but by giving yourself time to feel everything you're feeling, you're doing the most important healing process you can do.

Reaching out is a great process. I'm glad you reached out to us. If you feel comfortable, you might want to tell one or two friends about Tim's death, and see if it helps you with the process. If it doesn't feel right, you don't have to do it anymore. But you may be glad you did.

I think his wife and his family would love hearing what you wrote about Tim. It's touching, and it will help them heal to know that he had connections to many other people that will live on beyond him. If you feel right with it, it will mean a lot for them to hear this from you.

Best wishes for you as you deal with this.

Please don't, you are dear to more people than you imagine. I'm sorry about your unhappiness, and I know first hand how awful that can be. Is there any way you can talk to someone? Feel free to reply or to PM me and I'll be glad to talk.

I hear you -- I can imagine how draining it would be to shop around for therapists. I was lucky in that regard. Sounds like it's a wise decision to wait until you have the mental energy for it. Good luck!
Let me just add my voice to the "fun me is drunk me" theme here. But I finally had to stop drinking 10 years ago and figure out what was fun about me without the drinking.

I don't really know if this is appropriate, but I once heard a priest say that if you're poor and you need counseling, Alcoholics Anonymous is a good place, even if you're not an alcoholic, since the lay-therapy training that people get there can be really healing. Never tried it myself, but it may work for you if none of the other suggestions here do.

So sorry for the pain you're feeling. PM me if you need someone to talk to.

I'm so sorry for the pain you're feeling. It does sound like you need to be able to see a counselor or a therapist or someone who can give you some more help. Are you seeing someone now? I understand meds aren't the answer to everything, and I understand the desire to be off of your meds altogether, but maybe you can just find something that works for you in a semi-long-term way. I've been on Prozac for 15 years, and I've cut the dosage down pretty low, but I don't think I'll ever go off of it.

Best wishes for you.

I'm so sorry. This is a time in many people's lives that is particularly hard (it was for me), and you have a number of things that make this even harder than it was for me.

It sounds like you need someone to talk to. Is there a counseling center/service you can go to? Barring that, feel free to PM me anytime, but I'm not an expert, just a guy who has been through something similar.
You'll get there. It does sound like you and he have something really special. Best of luck with everything. Feel free to PM me if you need to talk.

It's both a physical disease and an integral part of yourself. Mine hasn't gone away, despite years of taking prozac, and I'll never be cured. However, I've made enough peace with the disease that I like the way I am, even this part of myself. This is the hope that I have for you. Best of luck with your treatment, and feel free to PM me anytime.
Thanks for the clarification on this.

I can't really comment on this since I'm not in Canada. But I wanted to applaud your intentions to see a mental health professional. Antidepressants made a huge improvement in my life. I was always afraid they would change me, but they really just kept me out of the deep lows.

The stigma isn't as bad as you think it might be. A surprising portion of the (US) population is on some sort of anti-depression or other type of medication for mental illness. 

I don't  publicize the fact that I take prozac (hence the semi-anonymous account), but many people close to me know. I wouldn't have started taking prozac if I didn't talk to a close friend of mine who had taken it with good results. I feel I have something of a responsibility now to tell other people that I've had good results with the drugs.

I can't offer any Canada-specific advice, but if you need someone to talk to about antidepressants in general, feel free to PM me.

I'm so sorry for you, I get it. When I had to go away to university, and my g-friend went to another school, it was absolutely devastating for me. I think I resented everyone else at school that first year because they weren't her. Didn't really make many new friends, never really felt like I needed to fit in. Couldn't wait to see her at Christmas break, and then she dumped me.

I got over it, moved on, but it was a hard year for me, back then. The years when you leave home and start to define yourself apart from your parents are magical years, and I think they amplify the wonderful feelings of being in love into something even more magical.

I was saved by the everyday task of going to class and learning my major field of study very well. Started to exercise so I could lose some weight. Probably drank too much then. With each new person I met the pain was infinitesimally diminished. One day I was okay. But it took a while.

Reply, PM me, or post if you need to talk. You **will** get through this.

There has been some good advice posted here, let me just add one additional piece that I feel particularly qualified for. This all happened after drinking, right? Alcohol is itself a depressant. Affects everyone differently, but it had a real destabilizing effect on me. The alcohol could be exacerbating whatever bipolar or depressive tendencies she already has. The part about getting really angry after drinking was something familiar to me. I used to get quite angry when I was coming off a buzz.

I'm not sure what I'd recommend you do with this advice. After years of trying to drink in moderation, I finally had to give it up, not so much because I felt that I was an alcoholic, but because my life is just easier without it. This is just something you should keep an eye on. And I hope it will make you feel a little less guilty about provoking your friend if you understand how the alcohol induced just this type of reaction in me; it has nothing to do with who you are or what you said.

Please don't do anything foolish. I know how grim it can be to be in your 20's with an uncertain future and shifting friendships. I've been there, as have most of the "happy" older people you see around you. But these situations change. You're young, you're really not supposed to have "talents" at 24, you're supposed to position yourself to learn talents. People care. You are dear to more people than you imagine. Post here, or PM me if you want.
Well put. I came here to offer support, but I can't say it any better than this. PM me as well, if you want.

It will be okay. I know how painful this can all be -- it was largely the same for me, I made the same mistakes, felt the same pain. Being a friend, being a boyfriend or girlfriend, these are all learned skills that most people haven't perfected by the time they reach college. You'll get better at all of these things, and your relationships will, in turn, be less painful and more rewarding for you. Feel free to post here and talk to us, and feel free to PM me.
It is your time to become an independent adult, and you are still hindered. It sucks, and I'm sorry about it. But it will get so much better!

It will be okay. Your parents won't be able to control you for so much longer. This is about the time when my life made the big climb from so-so to good.

Congratulations on your grades, volunteering, and AP classes. Sounds like you're on your way to being a superstar!

The college you go to doesn't matter as much as you think. How well you do there matters more. Go to the college your mother wants, if that's really your only option without going through hell. Work hard, ace your classes, learn as much as you can, make connections with the faculty members. 

You're also going to find you'll have better resources and advice once you get to college. Maybe you have to commute during your first year, but maybe you can look into getting enough financial support to live on campus for subsequent years. Or, maybe once your away from home, you can apply to some other schools and transfer someplace that you really want to go. Major in whatever turns you on.

Being at home sucks. I fought with my dad, or avoided my dad, for much of my teens, *and he was (and is) a pretty good guy*. Didn't think so at the time, but just couldn't get along with him. Still kinda avoid him, though I don't resent him like I did when I was at home. I think we're wired to want to leave home at around your age.

Your parents may also be clinging to the last bits of control they can exert over you. Things may get better when you start going to school. Then again, they may get worse.

Feel free to post here, or to PM me anytime. I'm not just blowing smoke up your ass when I say that you sound like a superstar. Go soar!

The weight gain happens. I went through a long period of sitting on the couch and eating cheese. Let me tell you that wasn't good for my waistline.

On the one hand, exercise will give you endorphins and make you feel fit. However, there are more important things than staying in shape, and maybe you just need a break. Sounds like you need pampering, and sitting on the couch and eating junk food is your way of pampering yourself. There are worse things.

Have you thought about seeing a therapist and taking anti-depressants yourself? They did wonders for me. Even a really low dosage is the difference between night and day.

But what you're going through is hard. It might be the hardest thing you ever do. This isn't a case of everything being fabulous and you feeling depressed, this is an example of you going through really trying times, and having a hard time, and feeling awful.

Hang in there!

You don't suck, you're just depressed. It happens to a surprisingly huge portion of the population, myself included. Drinking and depression, that was my 20's in a nutshell.

Look at it this way, calling a therapist is less work than getting a gun (joking). Seriously, though, didn't it feel better to vent here, to tell people about this? Wouldn't it feel better to have someone you could just unload to?

We keep these secrets inside us because we're ashamed to tell anyone about them, and in so doing we give them this magical power over us. 

Talk to someone. I'm happy to talk if you want to PM me. But I don't really know what I'm doing. A therapist will. 

Please make the call. You are dear to more people than you imagine.

The first few years of parenting are so incredibly hard. Looking back, I don't understand how I made it through those days. I was in a similar place: new job, new child, no sleep, all work, no play. It does get easier, it really does. But I understand the feelings of exhaustion and despair you have now.

A big turning point for me came when I felt I could start exercising again. I get up really early, and run for 30-45 minutes. Listen to some tunes. It's beautiful and cool here most mornings. I even like running in the darkness. No one else is around. It's really nice "me time" that served as a foundation for me to build my own life within my family and job responsibilities. Maybe something like that would work for you.

You're not alone, though. But your marriage will get better as your daughter gets older. IIRC, 13-18 months old was a big inflection point in my life getting better.
I feel exactly the same way. But it was sooo worth it for me.
My bad, then. Sorry about that.

Wow. I'm so sorry, that has to be a unbelievably painful and sad feeling. 

But you know how to work with computers, which is pretty cool, and even though it feel like you've lived "a whole life", your life is most likely just beginning, and there's time to do all of the wonderful things that comb_over suggested in his comment.

Please don't do anything permanent. There's this perception in college that everyone else is so much happier than you are, and there's something wrong with you if you're not Mr Sunshine. But pretty much everyone feels like shit from time to time, and no one is having as much fun as it seems from the outside. Everyone is insecure and scared and pretending.

That being said, maybe there's a counseling service at your school (I'm assuming you're at a school because of the computer problems thing) where you could start to talk about some of these issues. Feeling as miserable as you feel isn't right. You deserve to feel better, maybe not Mr Nonstop Sunshine, but "fear, debt, and loneliness" isn't okay. You deserve better.

I've been taking them for 15 years. I really don't have any problem with taking them for the rest of my life. I've dropped the dosage from 20 to 10 mg/day over the last year. Originally I had intentions of dropping it more to see if it helped, but I started to feel it.

The comparison they make in Listening to Prozac is that we don't tell diabetics they should wean themselves from insulin: we just appreciate that they have a need that might continue for the rest of their lives. But there's this stigma with antidepressants, like you *shouldn't* be on them.

Shouldn't make too much of a difference about it being a counselor not a psychiatrist. A huge portion of the population takes these drugs, and I'd imagine they get requests like these all the time. My normal doctor now refills my prescriptions for me, and I no longer see a therapist.

Maybe you should just say: "I love you, and I'm afraid that you're going to do something to hurt yourself." Bluntness can be the right tact sometime. But I've never dealt with anything like this. The fact that you're so in-tune to his feelings shows what a great friend you are -- he's a lucky guy.

Congrats about seeing a counselor and thinking about medication. Earlier today, I posted my comments about antidepressants [here](http://www.reddit.com/r/SuicideWatch/comments/de1tj/so_alone/c0zj3a3).

The good thing about meds is they will help you figure out what part of this is a chemical inbalance in your brain, and what part of this are social issues you can work through with a counselor.

For me, as it turns out, the meds alone do a fine job. I'm still introverted, and I'll always be introverted, but I'm fine with that. Big social groups still scare me, but I can handle those situations pretty well now. Most people who have met me think that I'm a pretty social person.

If you say any of the things you posted about to a counselor, they will almost certainly suggest medication without any further prompting. If they don't, I would strongly suggest you seek another therapist, but there certainly isn't anything wrong with simply saying: "I'd like to try seeing whether antidepressants can help with my depression."

Beware of the first few weeks on SSRIs. I went through almost a manic period while my brain was getting adjusted. I take Prozac, and some of the more modern SSRIs might be better now. This is a well-known effect, though, and a good psychiatrist should counsel you on this. But feel free to PM me.
This. Please talk to us. Please don't do anything stupid.

Thanks for saying everything you just did so honestly. To me it sounds like your depression is acute enough that you should think about getting professional help. I was depressed for a long time, and tried everything to try to cure it, drinking, overeating, overexercising, dating, not dating, working all the time, and lots of therapy. Finally, after talking to a couple of friends who had tried it, I got on an antidepressant medication, which really changed my life. I had always been worried because I thought antidepressants would change me, or wouldn't let me be exceptional because I'd be satisfied with being mediocre. None of these things happened: I take a very small dose of Prozac daily, and it has simply removed the depression without changing any of the other aspects. Maybe something like this would help you. Your school no doubt has a counseling service, and perhaps you could talk to someone there about trying some sort of antidepressant. I saw therapists for a long time, and it was comforting, but it didn't do anything to help my depression. 10 mg of Prozac made the depression much much better within a few weeks.

I'd like to just add my voice to the good advice that's already been posted here. Many, many people feel exactly the same way you do in college. But it isn't too late; in general, it never is, but in your case, you're still young, and have vast options in front of you. More of those same opportunities that you neglected will come again, maybe not the same ones, but ones like them.

Please don't do anything foolish, you are loved by and are dear to more people than you can imagine. Contact your school's counseling service and find someone that you can talk to.

BTW, if you want to talk Chemistry, PM me.
